[Resource from qmd at qmd://supabase/apps/docs/content/guides/ai/semantic-search.mdx] 210: 
211: ## pgvector index tuning
212: 
213: When working with embedding datasets at scale (100k+ rows), index selection and tuning can significantly impact query latency and accuracy.
214: 
215: Supabase uses Postgres with the `pgvector` extension, which supports two primary index types for vector similarity search: IVFFlat and HNSW.
216: 
217: ### IVFFlat index
218: 
219: **Best for:**
220: 
221: - Large datasets (100k-10M rows)
222: - Fast approximate search
223: - Lower memory usage
224: 
225: ```sql
226: create index on documents
227: using ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
228: with (lists = 100);
229: ```
230: 
231: ### HNSW index
232: 
233: **Best for:**
234: 
235: - High accuracy requirements
236: - Read-heavy workloads
237: - Low-latency semantic search
238: - Scenarios where recall is more important than memory usage
239: 
240: ```sql
241: create index on documents
242: using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
243: ```
244: 
245: ## See also
246: 
247: - [Embedding concepts](/docs/guides/ai/concepts)
248: - [Vector columns](/docs/guides/ai/vector-columns)
249: - [Vector indexes](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes)

For general advice about indexes, check out this [guide](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/22449). 13: 14: ## **To speed up queries, it is ideal to create an HSNW index on your embedded column** 15: 16: The general structure for creating an HNSW index follows this pattern: 17: 18: ```sql 19: CREATE INDEX ON USING hnsw ( ); 20: ``` 21: 22: Search can be one of three types: 23: operator | description | search type 24: -- | -- | -- 25: `<->` | Euclidean distance | vector_l2_ops 26: `<#>` | negative inner product | vector_ip_ops 27: `<=>` | cosine distance | vector_cosine_ops 28: 29: Queries can only use the index if it matches the search type used. If you are unsure which search type to prioritize, vector_cosine_ops is the most commonly used. You can checkout our [guide](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes) for more info. The folks at Crunchy Data also wrote an [explainer](https://www.crunchydata.com/blog/hnsw-indexes-with-postgres-and-pgvector) that you may find useful. 30: 31: Applying an index can be slow and computationally expensive, so there are a few preparations that should be made beforehand: 32: 33: **1. Make sure your pgvector is the latest available version on Supabase.** 34: 35: Versions 0.6 and later have accelerated HNSW build speeds. You can observe your current version in the [Dashboard's Extensions Page](/dashboard/project/_/database/extensions). You can perform a software upgrade in the [General Settings](/dashboard/project/_/settings/general) if necessary. 36: 37: **2. Setting up an external connection** 38: 39: The Dashboard has an internal time limit of ~2 minutes for queries. Indexing a large table will almost always take more time, so it is necessary to execute your code through an external interface, such as PSQL. 40: 41: You can install PSQL in [macOS](https://stackoverflow.com/a/49689589/2188186) and [Windows](https://www.postgresql.org/download/windows/) by following these links and instructions. 42: For Linux (Debian) you can run the following: 43: 44: ```bash 45: sudo apt-get update 46: sudo apt-get install postgresql-client 47: ``` 48: 49: Once installed, you can find your PSQL string on the dashboard by clicking [connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true). Make sure if you are using the pooler connection that it is the [Session pooler](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true&method=session) (port 5432). 50: 51: If your network can use IPv6, consider using the direct connection string instead of Supavisor. It's not mandatory, but for tasks that run a long time, it's best to reduce network complexity. To check if your network is compatible, use this cURL command to request your IPv6 address: 52: 53: ```bash 54: curl -6 https://ifconfig.co/ip 55: ``` 56: 57: If an address is returned, you should use your direct connection string found on the dashboard by clicking [connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true). 58: 59: **3. Increase memory for index creation (optional)** 60: 61: The `maintenance_work_mem` variable limits the maximum amount of memory that can be used by maintenance operations, such as vacuuming, altering, and indexing tables. In your session you should try to set it to a reasonably high value: 62: 63: ```sql 64: set maintenance_work_mem to ; -- '#GB' 65: ``` 66: 67: Inspect value to make sure it has been set: 68: 69: ```sql 70: show maintenance_work_mem; 71: ``` 72: 73: **4. Increase cores for index creation (optional)** 74: 75: The `max_parallel_maintenance_workers` variable limits the amount of cores that can be used by maintenance operations, including indexing tables. In your session, you should try to set it to a value roughly 1/2 to 2/3s of your [compute core amount](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk): 76: 77: ```sql 78: set max_parallel_maintenance_workers to ; 79: ``` 80: 81: Inspect value to make sure it has been set: 82: 83: ```sql 84: show max_parallel_maintenance_workers; 85: ``` 86: 87: **5. Setting a custom timeout** 88: 89: Disable query timeout for your connection: 90: 91: ```sql 92: set statement_timeout = '0'; 93: ``` 94: 95: Inspect value to make sure it has been set: 96: 97: ```sql 98: show statement_timeout; 99: ``` 100: 101: **6. Consider temporarily upgrading your compute size (optional)** 102: 103: If your task is particularly long, you can speed it up by boosting your computing power temporarily. Compute size is charged by the hour, so you can increase it for an hour or two to finish your task faster, then scale it back afterwards. Here is a list of [compute add-ons](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk). If you want to temporarily upgrade, you can find the add-ons for your project in your [Dashboard's Add-ons Settings.](https://supabase.green/dashboard/project/_/settings/addons) 104: 105: **7. Consider increasing disk size (optional)** 106: 107: HSNW indexes can produce temporary files during their construction that may consume a few GBs worth of disk. 108: Consider increasing the disk size in the [Infrastructure settings](/dashboard/project/_/settings/infrastructure) to accommodate for short-term disk stress. 109: 110: 115:

Root cause: your IVFFlat index (`lists = 100`) was built when the table had far fewer rows. IVFFlat's cluster count needs to scale with row count — as you cross ~250K rows, recall/plan quality degrades and query cost spikes, which is what's blowing past your client's SSL read timeout.

**Fix, per docs:**
- `apps/docs/.../guides/ai/semantic-search.mdx` §"pgvector index tuning" — for 100k–10M rows Supabase recommends switching to **HNSW** for low-latency search (IVFFlat is faster to build but degrades as data grows unless `lists` is retuned):
```sql
create index on first_table using hnsw (subtitle_embedding vector_cosine_ops);
```
- `apps/docs/.../troubleshooting/increase-vector-lookup-speeds-by-applying-an-hsnw-index-ohLHUM.mdx` — build it over a **direct PSQL connection** (not the dashboard SQL editor, which has a ~2min timeout), and first set:
```sql
set statement_timeout = '0';
set maintenance_work_mem = '2GB';  -- or higher
```
Given you plan to grow to 650K+ rows, HNSW will scale much better than repeatedly re-tuning IVFFlat's `lists`.
